>## Summary
>
>Adds a default-deny NetworkPolicy for the `openshift-console-user-settings` namespace as a CVO-managed manifest.
>
>This namespace stores per-user ConfigMaps for UI preferences but runs no pods. The default-deny policy is needed to satisfy the CIS Kube benchmark 5.3.2 requirement that all namespaces have NetworkPolicies defined.
>
>## What this PR does
>
>Adds `manifests/03-networkpolicy-user-settings.yaml` containing:
>- A `NetworkPolicy` named `default-deny` in namespace `openshift-console-user-settings`
>- `podSelector: {}` — matches all pods (none exist, but acts as a defensive baseline)
>- `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` — denies all ingress and egress
>- Empty ingress/egress rules (no traffic allowed)
>- Standard CVO release annotations matching other manifests in this namespace
>- `capability.openshift.io/name: Console` annotation for capability gating
>
>## Why
>
>Part of the [HPSTRAT-104](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/HPSTRAT-104) initiative to ship tailored NetworkPolicy resources with every control-plane operator by OCP 5.0. Even though this namespace has no pods, the CIS benchmark requires that NetworkPolicies be defined in all namespaces — the default-deny ensures that if anything is ever deployed here (by accident or maliciously), it has no network access.
>
>## References
>
>- Jira: [CONSOLE-5433](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONSOLE-5433)
>- Epic: [CONSOLE-5430](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CONSOLE-5430)
>- Feature: [OCPSTRAT-3495](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3495)
>
>## Validation
>
>- `make verify` passes with no diff
>

I don't think we [need](https://github.com/openshift/console-operator/pull/1195#issuecomment-5070854458) docs and PX approvers.  I don't see a need to doc this hardening specific to this repo, although I could see [OCPSTRAT-3495](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3495) as a whole having docs.  And this also seems like a top-down requirement, that even a hypothetically resistive PX representative couldn't block.  And I don't see anyone have a problem with us blocking traffic into or out of a Namespace that OCP owns and which will never run Pods.
